core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Pericarditis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes first-line high-dose NSAID therapy combined with colchicine to prevent recurrence, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sharp central chest pain that is worse when lying flat and relieved by sitting forward

Key HPI features: 24-hour history of sharp, pleuritic, retrosternal chest pain of sudden onset. The pain is 8/10 when lying supine in bed and taking deep breaths, but improves significantly to 3/10 when sitting upright and leaning forward. Experienced a sore throat, low-grade fever, and generalized muscle aches 10 days ago. Denies radiation to the jaw or left arm, and denies exertional worsening.

Objective/Exam findings: Auscultate heart: superficial, scratchy, high-pitched pericardial friction rub heard best at the left lower sternal border with patient leaning forward in expiration. ECG: widespread, diffuse ST-segment elevations with upward concavity (saddle-shaped) across multiple leads, plus PR-segment depression in limb leads (and PR elevation in aVR). Bloods: CRP, ESR, troponin (mild elevation possible if myopericarditis), FBC. Echocardiogram to exclude pericardial effusion.
Relevant background/PMH: none, no cardiovascular risk factors, no prior hospitalizations
Current medications: paracetamol 1g PRN with minimal relief
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Pericarditis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to ST-elevation myocardial infarction without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Breathlessness with distended neck veins — suggests tamponade.
management_principles: First-line therapy: high-dose NSAID (e.g., ibuprofen 600mg TDS or aspirin 750mg TDS for 1-2 weeks with PPI gastroprotection) combined with colchicine 0.5mg BID for 3 months to prevent recurrence
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: 2015 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases

reference_soap.subjective: 32M presents with acute pleuritic, postural retrosternal chest pain (worse supine, relieved by sitting forward) preceded by an upper respiratory tract infection 10 days ago.
reference_soap.objective: Auscultate heart: superficial, scratchy, high-pitched pericardial friction rub heard best at the left lower sternal border with patient leaning forward in expiration. ECG: widespread, diffuse ST-segment elevations with upward concavity (saddle-shaped) across multiple leads, plus PR-segment depression in limb leads (and PR elevation in aVR). Bloods: CRP, ESR, troponin (mild elevation possible if myopericarditis), FBC. Echocardiogram to exclude pericardial effusion.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute viral/idiopathic pericarditis. DDx: acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction (differentiated by diffuse vs territorial ST elevation and PR depression), pulmonary embolism, costochondritis, pneumothorax.
reference_soap.plan: First-line therapy: high-dose NSAID (e.g., ibuprofen 600mg TDS or aspirin 750mg TDS for 1-2 weeks with PPI gastroprotection) combined with colchicine 0.5mg BID for 3 months to prevent recurrence. Restrict competitive sports/strenuous exercise until symptom and biomarker resolution. Baseline echocardiogram to rule out effusion.

learning_objectives: Differentiate pericarditis pain from myocardial infarction based on postural relief (sitting forward) and pleuritic nature
Interpret the classic ECG features of acute pericarditis: diffuse concave ST elevations with PR depressions
Formulate dual anti-inflammatory therapy using NSAIDs combined with colchicine for recurrence prevention
Counsel athletic patients on exercise restriction during active pericardial inflammation

teaching.one_liner: Inflammation of the sac around the heart. The giveaway is pain that is worse lying flat and better sitting forward.
red_flags: Breathlessness with distended neck veins — suggests tamponade

must_ask.say: Is the pain worse when you lie flat, and better when you sit up and lean forward?
Does it get worse when you take a deep breath or cough?
Have you had a cold, sore throat, or fever in the last couple of weeks?

must_ask.objective: Site and radiation of the pain
must_ask.say: Where exactly is the pain, and does it move anywhere else?
When did it start, and how long does it last each time?
Have you become short of breath as well?

history.answer: Doctor, I have had a sharp, stabbing pain right in the middle of my chest since yesterday.
It started suddenly yesterday morning, about 24 hours ago, while I was resting at home.
It is right in the center of my chest, directly behind my breastbone.
It feels sharp and stabbing, almost like a knife piercing into my chest.
No, the pain stays right in the middle and does not spread to my jaw, left arm, or back.
It has been constant for the past 24 hours, rather than coming and going in spells.
When I lie flat on my back it reaches an 8 out of 10, but leaning forward drops it to about a 3.
Walking around does not make it worse, but trying to lie down flat in bed makes it agonizing.
Taking a deep breath or coughing makes it much sharper, and lying flat is awful, while leaning forward brings clear relief.
No, pressing on my ribs or breastbone does not trigger or worsen the pain at all.
Eating does not affect it, and I have not had acid reflux, sour tastes, or pain when swallowing.
I feel like I cannot take a deep breath because of the sharp stab, but I am not short of breath otherwise.
No, I have not had any cold sweats, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, or lightheadedness.
I do not have a cough or phlegm right now, though I felt feverish and warm last week.
About ten days ago, I had a bad sore throat, mild fever, and muscle aches all over.
No, neither leg is swollen or sore, and I have not had surgery, long flights, or prolonged bed rest.
No, there are no rashes, redness, or blisters anywhere on my chest or back.
I am anxious about my heart, but I have not had sudden panic attacks, trembling, or numbness in my hands.
I do not have high blood pressure, diabetes, or high cholesterol, and I have never smoked.
I have never felt chest pain like this before, and I have never had any heart tests or procedures.
No, I have not had any chest injuries, heavy physical blows, or unusual upper-body strain.
I wonder if that viral infection from last week somehow spread into my lungs or ribs.
I am terrified that I might be having a heart attack, even though I am young and fit.
I am hoping to get a chest X-ray and effective pain medication so I can sleep lying down.
I have never had any chronic medical conditions or health problems.
I have never had surgery and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I took one gram of paracetamol yesterday and again today, but it gave me minimal relief.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I only drink socially on weekends, usually two or three beers with friends.
I work as a secondary school teacher, live with my partner, and run marathons regularly.
Both my parents are healthy, and there is no family history of early heart disease or sudden cardiac death.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, heart rate 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 99% on ambient air, temperature 37.5°C.
Alert, oriented, sitting upright and leaning forward with comfortable appearance, but visibly hesitant to recline flat; no diaphoresis or pallor.
Normal jugular venous pressure without elevation, distension, or abnormal waveforms.
Skin is intact with no erythema, rash, or grouped vesicles along the chest wall.
Chest expansion is symmetrical without focal tenderness or reproduction of pain upon palpation over the sternum, costochondral junctions, or ribs.
Percussion notes are resonant and symmetric across all lung fields bilaterally.
Vesicular breath sounds are clear bilaterally with no crackles, wheezes, or pleural friction rubs.
Superficial, scratchy, high-pitched pericardial friction rub heard loudest at the left lower sternal border with the patient leaning forward in expiration; regular rate and rhythm with no murmurs.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender to light and deep palpation throughout the epigastrium and all quadrants, with no guarding.
No peripheral pitting edema in either lower extremity.
Both calves are soft, non-tender, and symmetrical without swelling, warmth, or cord-like firmness.
